newsitem.title: USA: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) May 1.
newsitem.headline: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) May 1.

text.p: Most global equity and bond fund managers stayed in the U.S. markets over the past two months despite stormy conditions generated by fears of more rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, a Reuters global asset allocation poll showed.
The average U.S. weighting of global equity funds slipped to 34.3 percent by the end of April from about 35.6 percent in late February.

The Dow Jones industrial average swelled to its life high at the close on March 11, reaching 7085.16. But the Dow plunged almost 10 percent about a month later, closing at 6,391.69 on April 11. The Dow surged again to close at 7,008.99 on April 30.

Within the global equities portfolio, the weighting of shares in Japanese, non-Japanese Asian, German, France, British and other European markets increased modestly while the weighting of Latin American and Canadian shares fell.
The average cash weighting of global equity funds rose to 3.4 percent from 1.9 percent.

Out of the global equity mix, Japan appeared to be the only sector that could offer value in the forseeable future, several survey respondents said, adding that they were optimistic about Japan's economic recovery.
Japan's global franchise firms, such as Mitsubishi Corp and Honda Motor Co Ltd, had benefitted from a weaker yen, exporting more goods abroad, they said.
But some analysts warned that Japan's troubled banking and property industries continue to weigh down overall growth.
Nevertheless, some U.S. buy-side managers said they were gearing up for a strong rebound in Japan's economic growth.

"Japan is getting ready for a buy signal," said Harry Clark, president of Clark Capital Management, and manager of over $350 million in assets. "We don't have it yet, but it is getting ready to go," he said.
On the fixed income side, managers pulled allocations from most major European and non-core European sectors and planted them back in the U.S. debt markets.
On average, U.S. debt allocations rose to 35.5 percent of assets from 30.2 percent, while the non-core European sector fell to 8.8 percent from 11.4 percent.
The volatile U.S. interest-rate scenario is not exactly beckoning investors to U.S. debt, fund managers said.

Despite the consensus forecast on Wall Street for one or two more interest rate hikes by the Fed this year, the U.S. debt markets offered a safe haven from shakier debt markets around the globe, they said.
Falling rates in Germany and France appeared to be barriers to entry, he said.
"France, Italy and Germany had their run for the roses," said Larry Daly, manager of the global fixed income group at John Hancock Funds.
"In Italy, we thought that the convergence (of interest rates) at the time-being had run its course," he said.
When asked about the U.S. debt, Daly said: "It is a little too early to get aggressive."
Country recommendations for the April survey were collected in late April.

Many of the respondents were still underweight U.S. equities when measured against the Morgan Stanley Capital International Market Capitalization Index, a widely accepted global benchmark.
"We've been underweight in the U.S. market on a global basis for quite some time," said Merrill Lynch investment strategist Lisa Cullen.
"Our view is that earnings should be slowing here and the economy will be slowing," she said.
For the most part, fund managers over the past two months weathered an extremely volatile U.S. equity market.
